newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Profit-taking trims Hungarian share prices.
newsitem.headline: Profit-taking trims Hungarian share prices.

text.p: Profit-taking trimmed Hungarian shares on Tuesday, bringing the BUX index down from Monday's all-time closing high, and analysts said a period of sideways trade was likely before new purchases in the autumn.
The BUX finished at a preliminary 6,753.95 points, down 41.05 points or 0.6 percent.

"I would not expect a lot more performance in the next few weeks or so, traditionally July and August tend to be fairly quiet months," said Nigel Rendell, Emerging European Strategist at HSBC James Capel in London. "It's more towards September time when people start to invest new cash," he added.
Rendell said the market firmed 42 percent in dollar terms in the first half of the year, adding that "it's the best return in eastern Europe with the exclusion of Russia."
Traders said on Tuesday investors cashed in some profits after recent strong gains.
"I think this 41-point fall was a result of profit-taking," said Peter Tolgyesi of Buda-Cash Brokerhaz.
"Intraday price movement showed that the market was fairly stable with serious demand for shares," he said, adding "this was convincing mainly in case of (oil and gas company) MOL.
MOL finished at 4,100 forints, down 50, after oscillating between 4,000 forints and 4,115 forints.
"Investors returned to (MOL's) market gradually," Tolgyesi said.
Elsewhere on the market, chemicals TVK finished at 3,300 forints, up 30; retailer Fotex ended steady at 209 forints and OTP Bank ended at 4,950, down 50.

HSBC's Rendell said he considered the market's longer-term outlook as positive, with the latest opinion polls showing senior governing coalition member Socialists ahead. He added that macro economic situation was also encouraging.
"The economic numbers, inflation and the current account have all been pretty good," he said, adding that interest rates were moving further down.
"For the end of the year we still forecast 7,500 (points) on the BUX -- that looks easily achievable now," Rendell said.
